newsitem.title: UK: IMRO probe finds catalogue of management failings.
newsitem.headline: IMRO probe finds catalogue of management failings.

text.p: British investments watchdog IMRO on Wednesday gave some indication of why internal failings at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management led to an embarrassing and costly debacle for its parent Deutsche Bank.

The Investment Management Regulatory Organisation published an in-depth summary of why it had fined two MGAM subsidiaries a record-breaking two million pounds ($3.3 million) and made them pay another million in costs for a catalogue of rule breaches and management failings.

This revealed that the two MGAM subsidiaries failed to notify IMRO about problems relating to the management of the European Growth fund and that at least one memeber of the MGAM board knew about the problems by April 1996, four months before the scale of the irregularities came to public attention.
These concerns included the fact that the risk profile and the investment profile of the fund were inappropriate and the overall profile of the fund was "getting out of control".
IMRO also found that the fund manager "persistently acted in a way that abided by the letter rather than the spirit" of unit trust rules despite giving several undertakings to change his behaviour.

The watchdog, which has been probing what went wrong at MGAM since September, said one of the fund subsidiaries had not organised or controlled itself to ensure its funds were properly managed and had not acted with due skill, care and diligence by failing to prevent funds from making investments in companies which were used to get around regulations.
And it found the other had issued promotion material for the Morgan Grenfell European Growth Trust, which along with the Morgan Grenfell European Capital Growth fund was managed by Peter Young.
Young was sacked by MGAM last September following the suspension of three funds and revelations of irregularities in the valuations of certain unlisted securites held by them.

He is currently under investigation by Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) but has denied any criminal activity. An SFO spokesman told Reuters that the IMRO announcement had no bearing on its inquiry, which was continuing.

The long list of failings at the MGAM firms detailed by IMRO includes them not having informed it of serious concerns about the management of the European Growth fund and not ensuring the funds were managed in line with the relevant restrictions.

Despite concerns about the inappropriate use of investment companies, an unusually high proportion of unlisted securities, the repeated failure of the managers of the funds to provide evidence of due diligence and their repeated attempts to exploit perceived loopholes in the regulations, Morgan Grenfell International Funds Management did not ensure managers were properly supervised.

Other concerns included the fund managers' inappropriate involvement in structuring investment instruments, their failure to take legal and technical advice, the arrangements for pricing certain securities and a breach of an investment guideline agreed with an institutional fund.
IMRO also found that MGIFM had failed to prevent its funds from holding investments which allowed an indirect exposure to the shares of certain companies above that allowed by the rules.

It also allowed these funds, which were held in special purpose vehicles, to be transferred into further such vehicles, maintaining this exposure. IMRO said the funds had invested a total of around 160 million pounds in these vehicles and one held five bonds "structured to exploit perceived loopholes in the relevant regulations". IMRO said it has yet to reach its conclusions about individuals responsible for the management and supervision of the funds in question. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
